J U D G M E N T
body: SYED MUDASSER AMEER, J. – Through this revision petition under Section 115, C.P.C., the petitioners have challenged the order dated 29.07.2025 passed by the learned District Judge, Kohistan Lower, in Civil Appeal No.03/13 of 2025, whereby their application under Order XXIII Rule 1, C.P.C., seeking withdrawal of the suit with permission to institute a fresh suit, was dismissed.

2. Briefly stated, the petitioners instituted a suit for declaration and permanent injunction, claiming ownership and possession of the suit property jointly with the pro forma defendants. The suit was initially instituted against seventeen defendants. Defendants No.1 to 3 contested it, while the remaining were impleaded as pro forma defendants. During the proceedings, certain other persons sought impleadment, which was allowed. An amended plaint was consequently filed, bringing on record persons belonging to eight different tribes. After framing of issues and recording of evidence, the learned Senior Civil Judge, Kohistan Lower, dismissed the suit vide judgment and decree dated 05.03.2025.

3. The petitioners challenged the judgment through an appeal filed on 27.03.2025. Respondents No.1 to 3 also filed cross-objections against the findings recorded by the trial Court on issue No.5. During pendency of the appeal, the petitioners moved an application on 26.06.2025 under Order XXIII Rule 1, C.P.C., seeking withdrawal of the suit with permission to institute a fresh one. The principal ground urged was that the relief of possession had not been claimed in the original plaint, whereas certain defendants had asserted their possession over the suit property in their written statements and evidence. The learned District Judge dismissed the application through the impugned order, hence this revision petition.

4. Arguments have been heard and the record examined. The question is whether omission of the relief of possession, in the circumstances of the case, constitutes a formal defect or any other sufficient ground under Order XXIII Rule 1(2), C.P.C., justifying withdrawal of the suit with liberty to institute a fresh one after its dismissal on merits.

5. Order XXIII Rule 1, C.P.C., provides two distinct remedies. Under sub-rule (1), a plaintiff may withdraw his suit or abandon a part of his claim. Such withdrawal, however, carries the consequence prescribed by sub-rule (3), which bars another suit on the same subject matter. Sub-rule (2), on the other hand, empowers the Court to permit withdrawal with liberty to institute a fresh suit where it is satisfied that the existing suit must fail by reason of a formal defect or that other sufficient grounds exist for permitting a fresh action. Such permission is not a matter of right. The Court must record its satisfaction on a legally recognizable ground.

6. In Muhammad Yar (deceased) through LRs and others v. Muhammad Amin (deceased) through LRs and others (2013 SCMR 464), the honourable Supreme Court explained the distinction between the two provisions. It held that permission to institute a fresh suit cannot be granted as a matter of course. The applicant must disclose reasons constituting a legally sufficient ground, and the Court must examine those reasons through a speaking order. The Court also clarified that where permission to institute a fresh suit is refused, the original suit should not automatically be dismissed as withdrawn, as the plaintiff may elect to continue with it.

7. The expression "formal defect" ordinarily refers to a procedural or technical deficiency which does not affect the merits or go to the root of the claim. A defect affecting the substance of the case cannot be brought within this expression merely by describing it as formal. In Muhammad Yousaf and others v. Nazeer Ahmed Khan (deceased) and others (2021 SCMR 1775), the honourable Supreme Court held that an inherent defect affecting the root of a claim is not a formal defect within the contemplation of Order XXIII Rule 1(2), C.P.C. The provision cannot be used to fill gaps in evidence or to provide a litigant another opportunity after an adverse adjudication.

8. The principle was further explained in Khawaja Bashir Ahmed and Sons (Pvt.) Ltd. v. Messrs Martrade Shipping and Transport and others (PLD 2021 SC 373). The Supreme Court held that the facts stated in the application must first constitute a ground recognized by law. Only then does the question of its sufficiency arise. A plaintiff cannot institute proceedings, withdraw them at convenience and reserve an unrestricted right to revive the same controversy through fresh litigation.

9. More recently, in Muhammad Ashraf and others v. Muhammad Khan and others (2025 SCMR 1066), the honourable Supreme Court considered an application for withdrawal of a suit with permission to institute a fresh one, moved during pendency of an appeal after the suit had been dismissed following a full trial. The Court held that the plaintiffs could not identify any formal defect warranting such permission and declined to interfere with the High Court's refusal. It observed that an unsuccessful litigant cannot be permitted to step back from an adverse verdict without disclosing a legally recognized defect in the suit. This principle squarely governs the present controversy.

10. The same distinction between an ordinary right of withdrawal and the special permission to institute a fresh suit has been reiterated by the honourable Supreme Court in Mst. Sakina Bi and others v. Barkat Hussain and others (PLD 2026 SC 177). The grant of permission under Order XXIII Rule 1(2), C.P.C., requires judicial satisfaction on the grounds prescribed by law. It cannot be claimed as an automatic consequence of a plaintiff's desire to abandon the existing proceedings.

11. This Court has also examined the expression "formal defect" in Gul Amin and another v. Haji Muhammad Akram (PLD 1981 Peshawar 72). It was held that defective drafting, non-joinder of parties or failure to produce documents do not, by themselves, constitute formal defects where the deficiencies can be addressed through the procedure available under the Code. Reference may also be made to Sharaf-ud-Din v. Abdul Wadood and others (2022 CLC 1282) and Bismillah and others v. Naik Muhammad through Legal Heirs (2024 CLC 262), which emphasize that the nature of the defect or sufficient ground must be specifically disclosed and judicially examined.

12. Tested against these principles, the petitioners' case does not satisfy either of the statutory grounds. In the original plaint, they categorically claimed ownership and possession of the suit property. Their claim for declaration and permanent injunction was founded upon that assertion. They did not plead that they had been dispossessed or seek recovery of possession. Now, after dismissal of the suit following a full trial, they seek to withdraw the proceedings to institute a fresh suit incorporating that relief.

13. Significantly, the application does not disclose when the petitioners were allegedly dispossessed, by whom, or under what circumstances. Nor does it identify any subsequent event which compelled them to seek recovery of possession. Their principal reliance is upon the assertions made by certain defendants in their written statements and evidence. An adversary's assertion of possession, by itself, does not establish that the plaintiffs were dispossessed. More importantly, it does not retrospectively convert an omission in the original plaint into a formal defect.

14. The omission is not merely procedural. A claim for recovery of possession requires a factual foundation concerning dispossession, its circumstances and the accrual of the cause of action. It may also raise questions of limitation and consequential relief. The petitioners have neither identified those facts in their application nor explained why the relief was not claimed when the suit was instituted or, at the latest, when the rival claims of possession emerged during trial.

15. Another relevant circumstance is that the question of ownership and possession was already part of the controversy before the trial Court. The issues framed, particularly issues No.4, 5 and 6, brought the rival claims of the parties into consideration. The parties led evidence and the learned trial Court adjudicated the dispute. The petitioners were thus aware of the defendants' stance regarding possession throughout the proceedings. Yet, no application seeking appropriate amendment was moved before conclusion of the trial. The request for withdrawal came only after the suit had been dismissed.

16. The stage at which the application was moved assumes particular significance. Although the mere pendency of an appeal does not exclude the jurisdiction to grant permission under Order XXIII Rule 1(2), C.P.C., the discretion must be exercised with due care. In Muhammad Yousaf (2021 SCMR 1775) and Muhammad Ashraf (2025 SCMR 1066), the Supreme Court cautioned against allowing an unsuccessful litigant to use conditional withdrawal to overcome the consequences of an adverse adjudication. The present application raises precisely that concern.

17. It is also material that respondents No.1 to 3 have filed cross-objections against the findings recorded by the trial Court on issue No.5. A fresh suit on substantially the same subject matter would prolong the controversy and subject the parties to another round of litigation. The respondents are entitled to have the pending appeal and their cross-objections decided on the record already produced. The discretionary jurisdiction under Order XXIII Rule 1(2), C.P.C., cannot be exercised merely to enable the petitioners to reconstruct their case after testing its strength in a full-fledged trial.

18. In Pehlwan and others v. Haji Muhammad Murad and others (2005 SCMR 1405), the honourable Supreme Court recognized that permission to withdraw a suit with liberty to institute a fresh one may be granted by an appellate or revisional Court where sufficient grounds exist, and that such permission is not confined to cases of formal defect. The principle is not disputed. However, the decision turned upon its peculiar circumstances, where a fresh suit had already proceeded to the stage of conclusion of evidence and permission was considered appropriate to avoid multiplicity of proceedings. It does not dispense with the requirement of demonstrating a legally sufficient ground under sub-rule (2). In the present case, no such ground has been established.

19. The possibility of seeking amendment under Order VI Rule 17, C.P.C., is a separate matter. Whether the petitioners can lawfully seek any amendment at the appellate stage, whether it would alter the nature of the suit, introduce a new cause of action or affect limitation are questions to be examined by the appellate Court if such an application is properly moved. No opinion is expressed on that question. The mere omission of a particular relief, however, does not automatically entitle a plaintiff to abandon a concluded trial and institute a fresh suit.

20. The learned District Judge has, therefore, committed no illegality, jurisdictional error or material irregularity in refusing the permission sought by the petitioners. The application disclosed neither a formal defect rendering the existing suit liable to fail nor any other sufficient ground justifying a fresh action. The impugned order calls for no interference under Section 115, C.P.C.

21. Consequently, this revision petition is dismissed. The order dated 29.07.2025 passed by the learned District Judge, Kohistan Lower, is maintained. The learned appellate Court shall proceed with Civil Appeal No.03/13 of 2025, together with the pending cross-objections, and decide the same in accordance with law. The observations made herein are confined to the application under Order XXIII Rule 1(2), C.P.C., and shall not prejudice the independent determination of the appeal and crossobjections on their merits.
Announced.
